questions.question: What is the law of effect? Explain it in the context of trial and error learning.
questions.solution_html:
• Thorndike's Trial-and-Error Theory of Learning. Trial and Error is a method of learning in
  • which various responses are tentatively tried and some discarded until a solution is attained –
  • stamping in of correct responses and stamping out of incorrect responses. 3 laws involved in
  • trial and error learning: Law of readiness - A satisfying state of affairs results when an
  • individual is ready to learn and is allowed to do so , law of exercise- law which states that, in
  • learning, the more frequently a stimulus and response are associated with each other, the
  • more likely the particular response will follow the stimulus., law of effect - states that those
  • behavioral responses that were most closely followed by a satisfying result were most likely
  • to become established patterns and to occur again in response to the same stimulus.

questions.question: Analyse how the neural network model explains memory.
questions.solution_html:
• Analyse how the neural network model explains memory.
  • Neural network models suggest that it is the rich interconnectedness of our neural units that
  • accounts for our ability to process information so quickly (see McClelland & Rumelhart,.
  • These models also propose that information in memory is not located in a specific place
  • within the brain; rather, it is represented by patterns of activation that spread over many
  • processing units and by the strength of the activation across these various units. The analogy
  • offered by Lindsay and Reed is spider web. Think of neural networks as being like a spider
  • web with millions of strands connecting various units. The tighter these strands, the stronger
  • the connections among various units. Incoming information "pulls" on certain strands, thus
  • activating other units, just as a fly that lands on a spider's web sends vibrations along the
  • strands to other locations—including the center, where the spider is located.
questions.final_answer: strands to other locations—including the center, where the spider is located

questions.question: Explain creativity ,its characteristics and stages.
questions.solution_html:
• The ability to produce work that is novel and appropriate. It should be original, unexpected
  • and useful one. It is a cultural, social and psychological event. The characteristcis include
  • Fluency is defined as the total number of suggestions you are able to make. Flexibility is the
  • number of times you shift from one class of possible uses to another. Originality refers to
  • how novel or unusual your ideas are. Divergent thinking is the reverse, in which many
  • possibilities are developed from one starting point.
  • The stages if creativity includes Orientation. As a first step, the person defines the problem
  • and identifies its most important dimensions. Preparation. In the second stage, creative
  • thinkers saturate themselves with as much information about the problem as possible.
  • Incubation. Most major problems produce a period during which all attempted solutions will
  • be futile. At this point,problem solving may proceed on a subconscious level:Although the
  • problem seems to have been set aside, it is still “cooking” in the background. Illumination.
  • The stage of incubation is often ended by a rapid insight or series of insights. These produce
  • the “Aha!” experience, often depicted in cartoons as a light bulb appearing over the thinker’s
  • head. Verification. The final step is to test and critically evaluate the solution obtained
  • during the stage of illumination. If the solution proves faulty, the thinker reverts to the stage
  • of incubation.
questions.final_answer: of incubation

questions.question: Define transfer of learning and different types of transfer.
questions.solution_html:
• Transfer of learning refers to the influence of previous learning on the acquisition or
  • performance of new learning. It explains how knowledge or skills learned in one context
  • affect performance in another. Transfer can be of three main types. Positive transfer occurs
  • when prior learning facilitates or improves new learning, such as when knowing how to ride a
  • bicycle helps in learning to ride a motorcycle. Negative transfer occurs when earlier learning
  • interferes with or hinders new learning, for example when habits of driving on one side of the
  • road create difficulty when switching to the opposite side. Zero or neutral transfer occurs
  • when previous learning has no effect on new learning, such as when learning mathematics
  • does not influence learning a musical instrument.
questions.final_answer: does not influence learning a musical instrument
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026
